designs.name: Handle Wall
designs.summary:
Handle Wall is a one-symbol, one-struct, all-handles bridge. `MbplAbiQuery(epoch)` returns a pointer to a single append-only function table; every parameter in it is a scalar, every function returns only `MbplStatus`, every string is a borrowed `(const uint8_t*, int32_t)` UTF-8 pair, every out-string is caller-allocated, and no allocator ever crosses in either direction. There is no `mbpl_free`, because nothing is ever handed over to be freed.

Everything the managed side holds is a `uint64` handle laid out as `kind | generation | slot`. The native handle table IS the ownership graph: each slot carries its `owner_slot` and an intrusive per-owner list, so `owner_of(h)` is O(1), teardown is a reverse-mint-order list walk, and there is no second structure that could disagree with the first. A mod cannot name itself — there is deliberately no `mod_open(mod_id)` — the host pushes the mod handle into `IMod.OnLoad(ctx)`, and that context is the only capability the mod ever gets. This is the same rule Stage 4's `execution.py` already enforces for item declarations, extended to the whole platform.

No-callback-after-unload rests on four legs: generational retirement (unload bumps every owned generation, staling every handle in existence); a per-callback re-resolve inside the dispatch loop, so a mid-dispatch teardown is visible on the very next iteration; deferred free gated on GameThread dispatch depth and per-slot pin counts, so a frame on the stack keeps its own storage while no new invocation can begin; and — the structural one — exactly ONE native-held function pointer in the entire system, an `[UnmanagedCallersOnly]` static in the host shim, never in a mod's assembly. Native therefore never holds an address inside code that can be unloaded, which is what makes the guarantee survive Stage 5's collectible ALCs rather than racing them.

Errors are result codes at the wall and nothing else: `0x80000000 | subsystem << 16 | code`, with symbol and detail retrieved from a thread-local last-error slot — the same `(code, field, detail)` shape Stage 2 already proved a loader can act on. The trampoline's body is wholly inside a `try/catch(Exception)` at the outermost managed frame, so an exception cannot reach `extern "C"`. In C#, expected outcomes return `ModResult`; contract violations throw `ModApiException`.

Compatibility is two layers, neither of them version sniffing: an ABI epoch that gates the structural shape, and a permanent feature registry (`misery.items`, `misery.input`, ...) where removal is a STATE rather than a disappearance — so a 0.5.0 mod on 1.0.0 is told "misery.items was removed in 1.0.0" and excluded by the resolver before its code is imported. Stage 4's existing `^0.5.0` semantics already deliver "runs on 0.6.0, refused on 1.0.0"; I add only feature granularity above it.

Every callback is on the GameThread, always, enforced by a thread-id compare at the top of every bridge function. Off-thread, only `Log`, `GameThread.Post`, and settings reads are legal; everything else is `MBPL_E_WRONG_THREAD`. A mod that blocks the GameThread cannot be preempted safely, so the framework detects, attributes, and quarantines: budget timing per callback, a `slow_callback` diagnostic naming the ModId, and after repeated violations a transition to `Draining` down the ordinary unload path. `PostAsync(...).Wait()` on the GameThread throws `deadlock_refused` rather than hanging.

Stage 5 can add Steam startup and CoreCLR hosting without touching any of this, because the managed layer is a caller of the table and never a member of it.
designs.left_out:
Ten omissions, each one safe because adding it is an APPENDED table slot plus a new feature id, and appending changes no existing signature, no existing offset, and no existing behaviour.

1. CORECLR HOSTING. Explicitly Stage 5, and the scope says so. What 4.5 fixes is that hosting cannot force a redesign: the managed side is a CALLER of the table, never a member of it, and the trampoline signature is already the one a collectible-ALC world needs.

2. SINGLE-MOD HOT RELOAD. Every contract required for it is here — `Draining`, generational handles, no function pointers into mod code, owner-scoped bulk teardown — but I am not shipping the reload path. It is later work in the host, not in the ABI.

3. UOBJECT / BLUEPRINT SURROGATE INHERITANCE. Stage 6. Deliberately absent so that no 4.5 signature ever has to be widened to admit it: any future surrogate surface is a new feature id with its own slots.

4. ARBITRARY BINARY SERIALIZATION FOR PAYLOADS. Only a typed property bag. Arbitrary serialization is a versioning bomb and a per-event allocation on the GameThread. If a real need appears, `bag_set_blob`/`bag_get_blob` are two appended slots and a schema id — additive.

5. GENERAL PERSISTENCE / SAVE-GAME INTEGRATION. Settings are a per-mod key/value store, nothing more. Save-game participation is unmeasured against this build, and the scope forbids inventing unmeasured systems.

6. PER-MOD SANDBOXING AND PERMISSIONS. Every loaded mod has the same authority. Ownership is already tracked per ModId on every single handle, so a permission bit is a field on the mod slot and a check inside the existing `mbpl_resolve` — precisely one function.

7. NETWORKING AND REPLICATION. Nothing measured, nothing invented.

8. THE CONSOLE UI. Only the registration foundation: name, help, args, print. The widget that draws it is a host concern and can arrive without any mod-facing change.

9. LOCALIZATION. Strings are authored literals. An `ILocalizer` on `IModContext` is an interface addition, not an ABI change.

10. RICH DIAGNOSTICS UI / PROFILER. `diag_snapshot_json` emits a machine-readable dump — handles per mod, subscription counts, callback budget violations, last errors. Anything that draws that is downstream and additive.

The one thing I would NOT defer, and did not: the trampoline signature and the pointer-ownership rules. Both are load-bearing for no-callback-after-unload and both are unfixable later without breaking every shipped mod. Everything above is deferrable precisely because none of it touches those two.

designs.name: Leased Context
designs.summary:
A DX-first, context-object bridge in which the mod's identity, its context object, and its ownership root are literally the same thing: one `MbMod` handle = `(slot_index << 32) | generation` into a native `FModSlot`. Every resource a mod acquires — subscription, input action, published or imported service, settings watch, item registration, console command, posted job — allocates one node on that slot's single intrusive LIFO ledger. Unload walks the ledger to empty, then increments the generation, which invalidates every outstanding handle for that mod at once in O(1) with no scan for stragglers anywhere in the process. Deterministic release is a property of the data structure, not of anyone remembering to call something.

No-callback-after-unload rests on four independent gates: a single native→managed chokepoint that revalidates the owner's slot generation and state immediately before *every* invocation (not once per dispatch); a synchronous `Live→Quiescing` flip, promoted at the top of the next drain when requested off-thread so it can never land mid-dispatch; an `inflight` depth counter (not a flag, because of reentrancy) that defers reclaim to a GameThread job once the stack unwinds; and a callback pointer that always aims at one `[UnmanagedCallersOnly]` thunk in the non-collectible host with a generation-stamped cookie as `user`, so native can never hold a pointer into unloaded mod code. Subscription *removal* takes effect immediately and synchronously mid-dispatch; *addition* takes effect on the next raise, mirroring the existing dispatcher's next-drain policy.

The ABI is one export (`mb_bridge_acquire`) returning a size-checked, append-only root table, with optional subsystems fetched as separate tables by opaque capability id — so a missing feature is a null table, never a number to compare. Strings are UTF-8 `(ptr,len)` borrowed for the call; outputs are always caller-supplied buffers; there is deliberately no `mb_free`. Event and item payloads pass named fields through accessors rather than structs, so adding a field is not an ABI change. Errors are packed `MbStatus` plus a sequence-checked, by-value `MbErrorInfo` with inline detail; C# sees a mechanically generated exception hierarchy for broken contracts and `Result`-shaped returns for contested outcomes, mirroring Stage 2's own split.

Not one ABI function accepts a mod_id string from a mod: `MbMod` is always first, local names follow. Stage 4's "a mod's code cannot name a namespace" is enforced by the shape of the C declarations rather than by a validator. Capability requirements live in `manifest_version: 2` and are arbitrated at plan time with a new fatal `missing_capability` diagnostic, so a 0.5.0 mod loads on 0.6.0 and is refused by name on 1.0.0 without ever comparing a version; at runtime required capabilities are plain properties and optional ones are `Try`-shaped only, making the negotiation a compile-time fact. Every callback is GameThread-only; `Post`/`PostAsync`/`SwitchTo` and `Log` are the sole thread-agnostic entry points, and everything else throws `WrongThreadException` off-thread. `EventArgsView` is a `ref struct`, so the compiler — not documentation — guarantees a mod cannot stash a payload handle past its callback.
designs.left_out:
DELIBERATELY ABSENT, each with the reason it is safe to add later. The general answer is that three things are extension points by construction: capability ids are additive strings, the function tables are append-only, and the ownership ledger is a tagged union with a per-kind release function — a new resource kind is a new tag plus one function, not a change to teardown.

1. PRODUCTION CoreCLR HOSTING. Explicitly Stage 5, per the scope. The bridge does not know a CLR exists; today the identical table is exercised from the Stage 4 Python harness through ctypes, which is the evidence that it is host-agnostic rather than the claim. Adding hostfxr changes only who calls `mb_bridge_acquire`.

2. GAMEPLAY EVENTS. Not one is defined here. `misery.world.day_changed` appears only as an illustration and would ship as `misery.diagnostics.tick` or nothing at all. The scope forbids inventing unmeasured events, and an event id that nobody measured is a promise the framework cannot keep — the same reasoning that keeps unproven fields out of `ItemDefinition`. Adding one later is a new capability id and, for existing mods, nothing.

3. HOT RELOAD OF ONE MOD IN A LIVE PROCESS. The ledger plus generation counters make it *mechanically* possible — that is exactly what unload already does — but nothing has yet proven that a collectible AssemblyLoadContext actually collects while native holds cookies into it. Claiming hot reload before measuring collection is how you ship a leak that presents as a slow memory climb over an hour. The design deliberately does not depend on collection succeeding: the no-callback guarantee holds whether or not the ALC is ever collected, because the thunk lives in the default context.

4. ASYNC EVENT HANDLERS. `EventArgsView` is a `ref struct`, so `async` on a handler is a compile error today. That is the deferral, made structural. An async handler's continuation resumes after the frame the event belonged to, which means the no-callback-after-unload guarantee would have to extend across a scheduler — a genuinely harder problem than the one solved here. When it is wanted, the shape is a separate `SubscribeAsync` whose continuations are ledger-owned resources cancelled by `ctx.Unloading`, which already exists.

5. A PERMISSION / SANDBOX MODEL. The undeclared-capability refusal (`MB_E_UNDECLARED_CAPABILITY`: using a capability the manifest did not list fails *even when the capability is present*) exists precisely so the manifest is a complete, static, auditable statement of what a mod touches. Turning that from an author-hygiene rule into a user-facing grant prompt is a policy layer over the same data — no ABI change, no API change.

6. BINARY PAYLOAD FAST PATH. Named-field accessors cost one call per field. If a measured event ever runs hot enough to matter, an appended `call_get_blob(call, schema_hash, void* buf, ...)` gives struct-speed reads with an explicit hash guard, and old mods keep using the accessors. Appending is free; starting with structs would not have been undoable.

7. TYPED, CODE-GENERATED EVENT PAYLOADS. `Subscribe<TPayload>` over a generated record is strictly nicer than `e.Int64("day")`, and the accessor ABI supports it unchanged. It is left out because generating types requires a stable event schema, and there is no measured event schema yet. Adding it later changes only `Misery.ModApi`, never the bridge.

8. NETWORKING, REPLICATION, SAVE-GAME PERSISTENCE beyond flat per-mod settings, UI/widget APIs, asset streaming control, and any cross-process diagnostics channel. All of these are new capability ids over the same lifecycle.

9. RESOURCE QUOTAS. `MB_E_LIMIT` is reserved in the code enum and never returned. Per-mod caps on subscriptions, items and log volume are trivial to add over `ledger_count`, which is already maintained. It is left out because no measured workload justifies a number, and an invented quota is a bug that only fires in a large install.

10. KILLING A STALLING MOD. Not an omission — a decision, stated under THREADING. The watchdog names the culprit; it does not abort the thread, because aborting mid-frame inside UE turns an attributable hitch into an unattributable crash.

designs.name: Lattice — a capability-negotiated native bridge for MBPL
designs.summary:
Lattice treats the entire mod-facing platform as a lattice of independently versioned CAPABILITIES rather than one API. There is exactly one exported native symbol, `MB_GetRoot`, returning a 32-byte `MB_Root` with three functions (`QueryCapability`, `AcquireCapability`, `ReleaseCapability`). `MB_Root` is frozen forever; it is the only thing in the system that can never change, and it is small enough that that promise is credible. Everything else — logging, events, input, settings, services, items, console, diagnostics, gamethread, and the host-control surface Stage 5 drives — is a named capability (`misery.events`, `misery.items`, …) served as its own `MB_<Cap>_v<major>` function table with its own MAJOR.MINOR. Two majors of one capability can be served simultaneously through a multi-year deprecation window, and a capability that does not exist yet costs nothing today.

Three mechanisms carry all the weight:

1. **The ownership ledger.** A mod is an `FModRecord` holding an intrusive LIFO chain of `FOwned{Kind, ReleaseFn, Subsystem, Payload}` nodes. Every capability that hands a mod anything pushes one release thunk. Unload walks that chain once, in reverse-insertion order. No subsystem is ever asked "do you hold anything of this mod's?" — which is exactly why adding a subsystem in 2031 does not touch the unload path.

2. **Epoch + generation, tested at the call site.** Handles are `slot:32 | generation:24 | kind:8`; every callback slot records `OwnerSlot` and `OwnerEpoch`. Quiescing bumps the mod's epoch, which invalidates every handle it owns and falsifies every dispatch predicate — atomically, and before any release thunk runs. Memory reclamation is deferred until `ActiveFrames == 0`, so a mod unloaded from inside its own handler is safe.

3. **One trampoline, forever.** Native never holds a managed function pointer. `MB_Callback{Invoke, Cookie}` is the only shape of any native→mod call, and for managed mods `Invoke` is always a single process-lifetime host trampoline; mod code is reached only through a table the host clears in unload phase 1. That is what lets Stage 5 add CoreCLR without editing one line of the C.

The public C# surface (`Misery.ModAPI`) is idiomatic — exceptions, `IDisposable`, generics, `in` parameters — and leaks no UObject, FName, ProcessEvent or address. A mod names a `local_id` and a content-relative path; `mod_id` is attached from the manifest by the framework, exactly as Stage 4's `execution.py` already enforces.

The bet: over ten years what kills a mod platform is not a missing feature, it is a breaking change to a surface that could not be versioned in isolation. Lattice makes every surface independently versionable on day one and pays one extra indirection per call for it.
designs.left_out:
Everything below is left out because it is either a NEW capability (purely additive: a new name, a v1 table, one line in a manifest) or a MINOR on an existing one (append a function, bump Minor). Not one of them requires changing `MB_Root`, the handle layout, the ownership ledger, the `MB_Result` encoding, the callback signature, or the threading rule. That is the specific claim the closing condition asks for, and it is the reason I froze the root at 32 bytes rather than trying to anticipate this list.

CORECLR HOSTING AND ASSEMBLY LOADING. Explicitly Stage 5, per the brief. Safe because the bridge only ever calls one trampoline whose pointer arrives via `SetManagedTrampoline`. Who supplies it — a C++ test harness today, hostfxr + a collectible AssemblyLoadContext tomorrow — is invisible to the C. Stage 5's remaining work is: resolve one `[UnmanagedCallersOnly]` method, hand it over, and gate `ALC.Unload()` on `ModIsReclaimable`.

ALL GAMEPLAY EVENTS. The event bus ships with framework events only (`ModsLoaded`, `ModUnloading`, `SettingChanged`, `ItemRegistered`, `ConsoleCommand`). Not one gameplay event is invented, because none is measured, and the brief forbids it. Adding `misery.events` event ids is a minor bump; adding a whole gameplay-facing surface is a new capability (`misery.world`, `misery.player`) whose v1 can be designed once there is evidence behind it.

EVENT PAYLOAD VERSIONING. A payload whose shape changes is a new event id in 4.5. Adding real versioning means adding a schema-negotiation function to `misery.events` — a minor. Doing it now, with one event producer in existence, would be designing against imagination.

SANDBOXING AND PERMISSIONS. Mods run with full process trust. Deliberate: the user chose to install them, and pretending otherwise while `Assembly.Load` exists is theatre. But the hook is already in place — capabilities are declared in the manifest and `AcquireCapability` refuses anything undeclared, so a permission prompt or a policy file becomes a decision inside `ModBegin`, not a redesign.

HOT RELOAD. Needs deterministic teardown to exist first, which is what this stage builds. Once `ModIsReclaimable` is trustworthy, reload is unload-then-load with the same `mod_id`, and the only new question is state migration — which is a settings/services concern, not a bridge one.

ASYNC/AWAIT AND ANY Task-RETURNING API. Needs a SynchronizationContext bound to a load-context lifetime; that is Stage 5's world. Additive as a minor on `misery.gamethread` plus managed sugar.

UI. No widgets, no panels, no HUD. Console is the FOUNDATION only: command registration, argument tokenisation, a text sink. No built-in command set, no autocomplete, no history UI. A real UI capability needs Slate/UMG contact this project has not measured.

BLUEPRINT SURROGATE INHERITANCE. Stage 6, untouched.

NETWORKING, SAVE-GAME INTEGRATION, ASSET STREAMING, LOCALISATION OF MOD STRINGS. Each is a new capability. Localisation in particular is deliberately deferred rather than half-done: `MB_Str` is UTF-8 everywhere, so a `misery.loc` capability can add lookup without touching a single existing signature.

SETTINGS SCHEMA MIGRATION. Settings are declare-first with a typed domain, so an unknown key on disk is dropped with a diagnostic and a changed type falls back to the default. Real migration (`OnUpgrade(from, to)`) is a minor on `misery.settings`.

RESOURCE QUOTAS BEYOND TIME BUDGETS. No memory caps, no allocation accounting, no handle-count limits per mod. Time is measurable today with the pump we already have; memory attribution across a shared CLR heap is not, and a quota you cannot attribute is a quota you cannot enforce. `misery.diagnostics` already exposes per-mod ownership counts, which is the honest half.

CROSS-MOD EVENT ORDERING BEYOND FIVE BUCKETS. No numeric priorities, no explicit before/after graph between mods. If ordering conflicts turn out to be real, the answer is a declared ordering constraint in the manifest resolved by the same topological sort Stage 4 already runs for dependencies — which is why I am not inventing a second ordering mechanism now.

MULTIPLE ABI VERSIONS. `MB_GetRoot` takes an `abi_version` and today refuses anything but 1. The parameter exists so that if the root ever must change — which I am asserting it will not — the mechanism is already shipped rather than retrofitted.

judgements.best: Leased Context — from the mod-author seat. It is the design where I can write the RadioMod end to end and have the type system, not documentation, catch most of my errors: optional capabilities reachable only through a Try method (so using an absent subsystem is a compile error), typed SettingKey<T>, typed inter-mod services acquired by contract alone with TryUse bounding the provider's life around my call, ref-struct payloads and a Compose builder that aborts itself if I forget to Raise, and await ctx.Game.SwitchTo() so background work has an obvious correct shape. Its failures are loud (ItemRegistration.Code, WrongThreadException, NamespaceViolationException) rather than silent, which matters more than elegance — a loud failure I fix, a silent one I ship. Its ownership reasoning is also the most rigorous on the question that actually decides the lifecycle guarantee: it names and rejects snapshot dispatch, revalidates before every single invocation, and states the removal/addition asymmetry instead of leaving it to be found. Lattice is the stronger engineering artifact overall — better ABI evolution (a frozen 32-byte root with independently versioned capability tables is the only design that can ship items v3 while log stays v1), better ownership edge cases, and the only correct answer to "what may OnUnload still call" — and if the question were "which survives ten years" I would name Lattice. But as the author, Lattice stops me at a compile error on its own framework events and hands me no async at all, and Handle Wall lets me write silently-wrong code in four separate places (ignored ModResult, unknown service method returning Success, typo'd capability string, unvalidated chord string) because stringliness is its premise rather than a bug. Leased Context's two real defects — a permissive AssetPath and a raw WorldClass string — are one-line type changes; the others' are their chosen shape.

scores.notes:
Cleanest leak check of the three: nothing in the public C# names a UObject, FName, ProcessEvent, IntPtr or address; ItemHandle is a private ulong with no accessor; ModAssetPath("Meshes/Radio") literally cannot express /Game/..., so Stage 3 namespacing is unstateable-wrong rather than validated. ModId has an internal ctor - unforgeable. Best threading story for a real author (IsCurrent, Post, PostAsync, TaskScheduler, SynchronizationContext) and PostAsync().Wait() on the GameThread throwing deadlock_refused is the single most author-protective detail in any of the three.

But it is the stringliest surface, and that is the design's premise rather than an oversight, so it is not fixable without changing the angle. Capability ids are strings (Has("misery.input", 1)) - a typo silently disables my feature. Chords are strings ("Ctrl+Shift+R") with no stated grammar, no stated clash policy, and Register returns IDisposable with no result, so I cannot tell a bad chord from a good one. Settings keys are strings. Services are a bag-based Invoke(method, args, result) with no method registry - and the design's OWN worked Tuner returns ModResult.Success for an unknown method, so "silently do nothing" is the path of least resistance for every inter-mod call I write. ModResult is a discarded-return-value type; C# will not warn me when I ignore it.

Two concrete holes an author hits: IServiceHandle.Invoke returns ModResult<ServiceResultView> and ServiceResultView is never defined anywhere in the surface; and the worked RadioMod's OnUnload calls _ctx.Log.Info(...) and _svc?.Dispose(), both of which must fail under its own mbpl_resolve, which refuses any handle whose owner state != ACTIVE while unload sets DRAINING first. My teardown logging silently no-ops.

Item surface matches execution.py's DECLARATION_FIELDS exactly (9 fields) but omits world_class, which Stage 2's ItemDefinition requires with no default - I cannot express a proven field.

The one I could sit down and write a correct mod in fastest, and the one where the compiler catches most of my mistakes. Optional capabilities are reachable ONLY through TryGetConsole(out var c) - there is no ctx.Console property to null-deref, so using an unavailable subsystem without checking is a compile error, not a runtime one. That is the best single "wrong thing is impossible" mechanism in any of the three. Typed SettingKey<T> statics, typed services by contract alone (TryGet<IRadioTuner> - I do not have to know who provides it), TryUse(t => ...) which bumps the provider's inflight so I physically cannot hold a dead provider's object, await ctx.Game.SwitchTo(), EventComposer that aborts on Dispose if I forget to Raise, and EventArgsView as a ref struct so the compiler forbids stashing a payload.

Its ownership reasoning is the sharpest of the three on the one question that decides the guarantee: it explicitly rejects snapshot-the-subscriber-list dispatch and revalidates before EVERY invocation, and it states the asymmetry (removal takes effect mid-dispatch, addition waits for the next raise) rather than leaving it to be discovered.

Where it loses my lens: AssetPath(string Package, string Asset) is a bare two-string record whose own example reads new AssetPath("/Content/Icons/T_Radio", "T_Radio"). The prose says relative-to-my-own-content; the type says nothing, and nothing stops me writing "/Game/Weapons/SM_AK". Both other designs made this unstateable and this one made it a runtime check - the exact class of thing my lens exists to catch. WorldClass = "WorldItem" is a raw engine class name with no enumerable legal values anywhere in the surface; I cannot write it correctly without reading framework source, and it is the closest any of the three comes to leaking an engine identifier into mod code. Event fields are stringly (e.Int64("day")), so field typos are runtime. IConsole, IDiagnostics and Transform are referenced but never declared. The illustrative misery.world.day_changed sits in the public sketch as if it were real, which the scope forbids inventing. TryGetConsole/TryGetDiagnostics as hand-written per-capability methods does not scale, though only the framework implements IModContext so adding one is source-compatible for mods.

Makes the wrong thing hardest at the type level and has by far the best evolution story. Capabilities are generic and typed - Require<IItems>() and TryGet<IConsole>(out var c) - so there is no capability string to typo and no version number anywhere in mod code; Supports(EventsFeature.CancellableEvents) covers within-capability features without a minor comparison. Declare-first settings with a domain and a label (DefineInt("volume", 50, 0, 100, "Radio volume")) are the only ones of the three that a settings UI or console could enumerate without loading me. Items Register THROWS by default with TryRegister for bulk, which is the right default - the common path fails loudly and I opt into quiet. AssetRef.Own is relative-only. The input clash policy is the only well-reasoned one on offer: a keybind collision registers UNBOUND with IsBound == false rather than refusing my mod, while an item collision refuses - and it says why. LEAKED as a distinct mod state when a release thunk fails mirrors registry.py's rule about keeping a registration when dematerialize fails. OnUnloading runs while the mod is still Live, BEFORE quiescing, which is the correct resolution of the problem Handle Wall trips over.

What stops me on day one: ModEventHandler<T> and Declare<T> both require T : unmanaged, and three of its own five shipped framework events (ModUnloading, ItemRegistered, and anything carrying ModId) hold a string and therefore cannot satisfy it. As written the public event surface does not compile, and the constraint also means no event I raise can ever carry text - a real expressiveness gap the design never acknowledges. Second: there is no async at all - IGameThread is IsCurrent, Post(Action), AssertCurrent - so my "parse a file on a worker and come back" code has no idiomatic shape. Third: the summary says ModId is "never authorable by mod code" and then the worked example writes new ModId("alphamod") to consume a service, and subscribes via events.TryOpen<ModsLoaded>(ModId.Framework, ...) where ModId.Framework is never declared and the ternary passes default(EventChannel<T>) to Subscribe with undefined behaviour. Fourth: it deliberately gives ^ a different meaning for capabilities (>=0.5 <1.0) than Stage 4's semver gives framework_api - two comparators sharing one syntax in one manifest is a trap that produces a wrong load decision quietly. It pays for that honestly, but I am the one holding both rules.

judgements.fatal_flaws:
STAGE-5-FORCING. (A) Handle Wall and Leased Context both ship a Task-returning surface in the 4.5 public C# API before the hosting model exists — Handle Wall exposes TaskScheduler and SynchronizationContext outright, Leased Context exposes PostAsync and GameThreadAwaitable SwitchTo(). An awaited continuation is a callback that neither design's ownership ledger mints: both ledgers own only what crosses the ABI, and a continuation is created by the CLR. Both state "no callback may target unloaded mod code" and enforce it for events, input, settings, console, services and posted jobs, and neither states that a continuation resumed on the GameThread scheduler is ledger-owned or epoch-gated. A SynchronizationContext's lifetime is also bound to the ALC that created it. If Stage 5 finds that continuations must be re-shaped or removed, that is a change to the public C# API shape, which the closing condition explicitly forbids. Lattice is the only design that avoids this, by shipping no Task-returning API and saying why. This is the single sharpest forward-compat difference among the three.

(B) Handle Wall's mbpl_resolve refuses any handle whose owner state is not ACTIVE, and unload sets DRAINING before anything else. It is the only design where I could add hostfxr + CoreCLR + per-mod collectible ALCs + Steam startup by writing host code and touching nothing in the bridge. `misery.host` already contains SetManagedTrampoline, ModBegin (negotiating capabilities before mod code loads), ModUnload, and — uniquely — ModIsReclaimable, which is the exact predicate AssemblyLoadContext.Unload() has to gate on and which the other two force me to synthesize or append. MB_UnloadReport and MB_MODSTATE_LEAKED give me evidence and a named state for the specific way Stage 5 fails (an ALC that will not collect). Async is deferred to me with the reason stated correctly, so no public Task/SynchronizationContext contract is pre-committed before the ALC lifetime question is answered. A 32-byte frozen root plus independently versioned capability tables means any host operation Stage 5 turns out to need is a MINOR on misery.host, not an epoch bump for the whole platform. Handle Wall has the better ABI mechanics and the cleaner ownership array; Leased Context has the better C# ergonomics; neither of those is what the closing condition is about.

scores.notes: The best ABI *mechanics* of the three and the worst host story. All-scalar parameters mean my entire binding layer is `delegate* unmanaged[Cdecl]<...>` with zero marshalling, zero aggregate-by-value questions, and SuppressGCTransition available on the cheap calls. Nothing else comes close on that axis. But the table contains NO host-control surface: no `mod_begin`, no `mod_activate`, and critically no `mod_is_reclaimable`. The design says the host PUSHES the mod handle via MBPL_OP_MOD_LOAD — but at Stage 5 I AM the host, and there is no function I can call to create a mod slot from a resolved load plan, nor to ask whether ALC.Unload() is safe. `gt_depth()` is process-global and per-slot `pin_count` is not queryable, so I cannot even synthesize the gate. Each is an appended slot (rev 2, no offsets move, no shipped mod breaks), so it is not a redesign — but the closing condition is that the contracts be SUFFICIENT for Stage 5, and as written they are not. Second: `IGameThread` publicly ships `TaskScheduler` and `SynchronizationContext` at 4.5. A SynchronizationContext is a process-lifetime object; a mod's `await` captures it and parks a continuation pointing into the collectible ALC. Implementable behind the same public shape (per-mod SyncContext as a ledger resource, fault pending continuations at Draining), but it is a public C# commitment made before anyone measured what collectible-ALC continuations do. Third: no reentrancy depth cap; managed frames are far fatter than C++ frames and a raise chain that is fine in the native harness can overflow the GameThread stack in Shipping. Strengths I would keep: the handle table IS the ownership graph (one array, no second structure that can disagree — the tightest ownership story here), and the property-bag `service_invoke` is the only inter-mod service design of the three immune to cross-ALC type identity, because no Type ever crosses. TLS last-error is correct if fetched synchronously and the wrapper does, but it is a strictly worse contract than a caller-allocated error struct.

Best DX of the three by a clear margin, and it does have a host surface: `mod_open` (host-only), `mod_activate`, `mod_begin_unload` (callable from any thread, promoted at the top of the next drain — genuinely useful when a worker-thread crash handler must stop a mod), `mod_inflight`, `mod_owned_count`, `token_release`. No `mod_is_reclaimable`, but I can build the ALC gate from `inflight == 0 && owned_count == 0`, which is serviceable. Optional capabilities being Try-shaped ONLY — no `ctx.Console` property to null-deref — makes misuse a compile error rather than a runtime one; that is the single best individual idea in any of the three sketches. Stage 5 problems: (1) `IServices.Publish<TService>` requires TService to live in a shared contract assembly in the default load context — the right call, and one I would make too — but manifest_version 2 as defined declares only `assemblies` and `entry`, so the design depends on a manifest concept it never defines. Additive, but it becomes my problem to discover. (2) `ServiceRef<T>.TryUse(Action<T>)` hands the consumer the provider's real object; nothing stops it being stashed in a static, rooting the provider's ALC forever. IsAlive goes false; the assembly never collects. (3) `PostAsync` returns Task, and a post whose owner quiesces is 'dropped, not run' — leaving the TaskCompletionSource permanently incomplete, which roots the mod's async state machine inside the collectible ALC, so ALC.Unload() never completes. The design has a rigorous answer for the native side of unload and no answer at all for the managed continuation side. (4) `MbStr` crosses by value; on win-x64/__cdecl a 16-byte struct goes by hidden pointer and CoreCLR implements that correctly, but it is a marshalling correctness surface I must validate that Handle Wall simply does not have. The `MbErrorInfo.sequence` check — refuse to attach a detail whose sequence does not match the call just made — is a sharp answer to the GetLastError staleness trap, though a per-call MB_Err* beats it outright.

The only one of the three written by somebody who thought about my job specifically. `misery.host` gives me exactly the four calls I need — `SetManagedTrampoline` (once, process lifetime), `ModBegin(mod_id, caps[], out_mod)` which resolves capability negotiation BEFORE a byte of mod code loads, `ModUnload`, and `ModIsReclaimable`, documented as the single thing AssemblyLoadContext.Unload() gates on. `MB_UnloadReport{Released, Leaked, DroppedCallbacks, ActiveFramesAtRequest, ReclaimDeferred}` is the acceptance artefact Stage 5 needs and nobody else produces. `MB_MODSTATE_LEAKED` — slot never recycled, epoch never reissued — is a named state for the exact Stage 5 failure I expect (an ALC that will not collect because one root survived); the other two have no vocabulary for it. Async/await is deliberately absent from 4.5 with the reason stated correctly — 'needs a SynchronizationContext whose lifetime is tied to a load context, which is Stage 5's problem' — so I design that with the ALC in hand instead of honouring a public Task surface written before the question was asked. The depth-8 reentrancy cap is the only bound on GameThread stack growth in any of the three, and it matters more once managed frames are in the chain. The seqlock `MB_CurrentDispatch` read from a separate watchdog thread is the only mechanism that still names a culprit when the GameThread is fully hung — at Steam-startup time that is the difference between a bug report and a shrug. Per-capability tables cost me ~150 lines of acquire-and-cache in the host and buy independent versioning forever; a 32-byte frozen root is a promise small enough that I believe it, which is not true of a 60-slot monolith. Real flaws: (1) `ModEventHandler<T> where T : unmanaged` collides with its own shipped framework events — `ModUnloading{ModId Mod}` and `ItemRegistered{ModId Owner}` are not unmanaged, because ModId holds a string. Fixing it means touching the identity type, which is precisely what must not move. Fix at 4.5 review, not at Stage 5. (2) The unmanaged constraint means event payloads cannot carry strings at all — a serious practical limit for a general event bus that the design never acknowledges. (3) `MB_Str` crosses by value in the FROZEN root (QueryCapability); if aggregate-by-value ever bites, it bites the one thing promised never to change. (4) Two ownership structures (FOwned slab + FSubSlot table) that can in principle disagree; Handle Wall's single unified array is tighter. (5) `LogField.Of(...)` params-array logging is verbose next to interpolated strings.

judgements.best: Lattice. Under an adversarial lifecycle lens the decisive question is not "which mechanism is most elegant" but "when a malicious mod P/Invokes the exported symbol directly, can the runtime refuse it?" — because the C ABI, not the C# API, is the real boundary in an in-process mod host. Lattice is the only design where the answer is mostly yes: `MB_ModHandle owner` is the first parameter of nearly every mutating call, so cross-mod violations are checkable, and the host-control surface (SetManagedTrampoline, ModBegin, ModUnload) lives behind a `misery.host` capability that AcquireCapability refuses to non-host owners. Handle Wall cannot perform the check at all — `mod_unload(mod, reason)`, `event_unsubscribe(sub)`, `item_unregister(item)` carry no caller identity and native has no ambient current-mod, so MBPL_E_NOT_OWNER is a defined-but-unreachable code; fixing it means rewriting most of the table. Leased Context is close to Lattice but ships `mod_open(mod_id)` in the mod-reachable root table, a one-call identity-forgery primitive that falsifies its own central claim. Lattice also has the best lifecycle semantics (OnUnloading-before-quiesce with no OnUnloaded; MB_E_MOD_QUIESCING on re-entry during teardown; a LEAKED state whose slot and epoch are never reissued) and the only explicitly named Stage 5 gate, ModIsReclaimable. Tiebreaker on the flaws: Lattice's worst hole (per-subscription MB_InvokeFn) is a one-field deletion today, while Handle Wall's worst hole (no owner parameter anywhere) is a table-wide rewrite. Reversibility decides it.

scores.notes: BEST MECHANISM, WEAKEST AUTHORIZATION. Its single strongest idea in the whole set: subscriptions carry `uint64 target`, not a function pointer, so the ABI *cannot express* 'native holds an address inside code that can be unloaded'. That makes no-callback-after-unload structural rather than a race, and it is the one property Stage 5's collectible ALCs actually need. Tombstone-now / free-at-depth-zero (generation bump synchronous, dispose() deferred via pending_free gated on g_gt_depth + pin_count) is the correct two-phase split and is the only one shown as real code. ATTACKS THAT LAND: (1) AUTHORIZATION IS INEXPRESSIBLE. `event_unsubscribe(sub)`, `item_unregister(item)`, `handle_release(any)`, `bag_set_*(bag,...)`, `settings_*(store,...)` and above all `mod_unload(mod, reason)` take NO caller identity. `mbpl_resolve` checks kind/generation/alive/owner-state but never 'is the caller the owner'; there is no ambient current-mod on the native side and there cannot be. MBPL_E_NOT_OWNER is defined and unreachable. Any mod P/Invokes the exported MbplAbiQuery directly (it is __declspec(dllexport); the C# wrapper is not the boundary) and brute-forces handles — slots are small ints and generations start near zero, so ~2^18 probes finds a live victim handle. Result: cross-mod unsubscribe, cross-mod item unregister, cross-mod settings write, and mod_unload of every other mod. Fixing this means adding an owner parameter to most of the table, i.e. rewriting the table. (2) `host_set_trampoline(MbplTrampolineFn)` sits in the same mod-reachable table with no host gate and no stated one-shot latch: a mod installs its own function pointer and owns every callback in the process, for every mod. (3) `IServiceHandle.TryGetDirect<T>(out T)` hands a consumer a raw managed reference to another mod's implementation with no lease, no epoch check and no revocation — it roots the provider's ALC and lets the consumer call into a dead mod forever. This directly falsifies the design's own headline guarantee, in its own public C# API. (4) The one true predicate is wrong: `mbpl_resolve` returns null unless owner state == MBPL_MOD_ACTIVE, but states are Loading -> Active -> Draining, so every call from OnLoad fails — the worked RadioMod example does not work. Symmetrically, teardown sets DRAINING before the walk and the pseudocode never invokes MBPL_OP_MOD_UNLOAD at all, so OnUnload's `_ctx.Log.Info(...)`/`_svc?.Dispose()` are inert or unsequenced. (5) Off-thread `settings` READS are declared legal while the GameThread is mutating slots and bumping generations during teardown; no synchronization is specified anywhere. This is the widest off-thread window of the three. (6) 24-bit generation: a mod hammering subscribe/unsubscribe wraps a slot's generation in ~17M cycles and resurrects a saved stale handle (ABA). Unaddressed. ABI craft is the best in the set — all scalars, no aggregates, no arrays, no allocator, one symbol, one struct, epoch + append-only revision. Ergonomics suffer because every optional subsystem is a non-null property you must remember to guard with Capabilities.Has().

BEST DX, BEST OFF-THREAD UNLOAD REASONING, ONE SELF-FALSIFYING FUNCTION. Correctly rejects snapshot dispatch and revalidates per invocation, so a subscription retired at index 3 while the loop sits at index 1 is genuinely skipped. `inflight` as a DEPTH not a flag is right for reentrancy. The best single piece of threading analysis in the set: off-thread `mod_begin_unload` sets an atomic and the pump promotes Live->Quiescing at the TOP of the next drain, so a state flip can never land between two subscribers of one dispatch. Ledger walk is `while (head)` — walk-to-empty, so a resource pushed by a release thunk is still collected (Handle Wall's reverse-walk-from-tail and Lattice's LIFO walk both risk missing one). ATTACKS THAT LAND: (1) FATAL, AND SELF-INFLICTED: `mb_bridge_acquire` is exported, and the root MbBridge contains `mod_open(MbStr mod_id, MbMod* out_mod)` guarded by nothing but the comment `/* host only */`. The summary claims 'Not one ABI function accepts a mod_id string from a mod' — this one does, and it is the identity-forgery primitive. A mod P/Invokes it with a victim's mod_id, receives that mod's ownership root, and can then subscribe/register/settings-write AS the victim and call `mod_begin_unload` on it. Every namespace guarantee in Stages 2-4 becomes advisory. (2) `MbCallbackFn fn, void* user` on `subscribe`, `action_register`, `watch`, `on_available`, `command_add` and `gt_post` means the ABI *permits* a mod to hand native its own [UnmanagedCallersOnly] pointer from a collectible ALC — precisely the use-after-free the design rejects in its own REJECTED #3. The host thunk convention is not enforced by the C. Removing `fn` later is an ABI break. (3) `token_release(MbToken)` and every `call_get_*` take no owner, so guessed tokens release other mods' resources and read other mods' in-flight payloads. (4) `ServiceRef<T>.TryUse(Func<T,R> body, out R result)` — call it as `TryUse(t => t, out var stashed)` and the lease is over: you hold the provider's object, it roots the provider's assembly, and the inflight guard never runs again. `TryUse(Action<T>)` has the same hole via lambda capture. T is a class, not a ref struct; nothing in the type system stops it. (5) `mod_begin_unload` returns before quiescence is complete, so a worker thread that acts on success proceeds against a still-Live mod. (6) 32-bit generation is the best of the three (~256x more ABA headroom than HW/Lattice) but still unbounded-churn reachable and undiscussed. (7) `public readonly ref struct EventComposer : IDisposable` requires C# 13 ref-struct interfaces; `EventArgsView` as a ref struct is genuinely the right call and the best use of the compiler as an enforcement mechanism in the set. Ergonomics are the best on offer: Try-shaped optional capabilities so an unchecked optional is a COMPILE error, typed SettingKey<T>, `await ctx.Game.SwitchTo()`, and a stated exception/result split that mirrors registry.py.

THE ONLY DESIGN WHERE OWNERSHIP VIOLATIONS ARE CHECKABLE, AND THE BEST LIFECYCLE SEMANTICS. Nearly every mutating entry takes `MB_ModHandle owner` first — `Unsubscribe(owner, sub)`, `UnregisterAction(owner, action)`, `Unregister(owner, item)`, `SetScalar(owner, h, ...)`, `Revoke(owner, h)` — so 'this handle is not yours' is expressible and enforceable, which is the axis both rivals fail. Host control is a separate capability (`misery.host`) that AcquireCapability refuses to any non-host owner, so there is no mod_open and no ungated trampoline installer in the mod-reachable surface. Best lifecycle reasoning in the set on three points nobody else gets right: `OnUnloading` runs while the mod is still Live and there is deliberately no OnUnloaded (Handle Wall walks straight into that trap); re-entering the framework during your own teardown returns MB_E_MOD_QUIESCING rather than silently registering a resource the walk has already passed; and a failed release thunk moves the record to LEAKED, whose slot is never recycled and whose epoch is never reissued, so no future mod inherits a leaked identity. `ModIsReclaimable` (ActiveFrames==0 AND ledger empty AND host table cleared) is the only explicitly named gate for Stage 5's ALC.Unload() — that alone is most of the closing condition. ATTACKS THAT LAND: (1) `MB_Callback { MB_InvokeFn Invoke; uint64_t Cookie; }` on every Subscribe/OnAction/OnChanged/RegisterCommand/Post. The design's REJECTED #3 correctly forbids managed function pointers, then its own header lets a mod supply one — `MB_GetRoot` is exported, so a mod P/Invokes Subscribe with its own [UnmanagedCallersOnly] thunk and native now holds an address in a collectible ALC. Only Handle Wall's cookie-only shape makes this inexpressible. Fixable NOW by dropping Invoke from MB_Callback; an ABI break later. (2) Callbacks receive `const void* payload, int32 payload_size` — the only raw pointer handed to mod code anywhere in the three designs. Combined with (1), a native-callback mod stashes it and reads freed memory after the raise returns. (3) SYNCHRONOUS LEDGER WALK WITH A MOD FRAME ON THE STACK. The answer states release runs immediately even when ActiveFrames >= 1 'because releasing only tombstones slots'. That is an unstated, unenforced invariant binding every future subsystem's ReleaseFn ('never free anything a live frame can reach') — and the raw payload pointer in (2) is exactly such memory. Handle Wall's pin_count/pending_free and Leased Context's deferred reclaim are both safer here. (4) `ServiceRef<T>.Target` returns a plain managed reference; the epoch check happens on the property access, not on subsequent use, so `var t = grid.Target;` caches past revocation and roots the provider's ALC. It reads as a property you are meant to cache, which is worse than TryUse. (5) 24-bit epoch/generation: same ABA-by-churn exposure as Handle Wall. (6) Reads lack owner (`GetScalar`, `GetString`, `CheckAlive`, `IsBound`, `GetRowName`) so handle-guessing still leaks other mods' state — low severity, but it undercuts the otherwise-complete owner discipline. (7) SLOPPINESS WHERE IT IS FATAL: `static_assert(sizeof(MB_Field) == 32)` is wrong — MB_Str(16) + uint8(1) + _Pad[7] + union{int64,double,MB_Str}(16) = 40 on x64. A wide by-value struct surface is exactly where this class of error is unrecoverable, which is the honest cost of the largest boundary-struct inventory in the set. (8) `IModLog : ICapability` puts `Major`/`Minor` on every interface a mod touches, inviting the version sniffing the design forbids. Also carries real complexity debt: two semver comparators (capability ^0.5 == >=0.5 <1.0 vs Stage 4's caret) is a live footgun for the 62 passing offline tests it is careful not to change.

synthesis.recommended_shape:
**MBPL Bridge v1 — "Lattice, hardened."** Start from Lattice (highest forward-compat and ABI-stability scores), graft Handle Wall's ABI mechanics and Leased Context's compile-time safety, and delete every construct the judges could attack.

THE WHOLE SYSTEM IS SIX CONCEPTS. Everything below is an instance of one of them.

1. **One export, one root, one token.** `MbAcquireRoot(abi_version, token, token_len, &root)` returns a 32-byte `MbRoot` with exactly three functions: `query_capability`, `acquire_capability`, `release_capability`. `MbRoot` is frozen forever — it is small enough and dumb enough that the promise is credible, which is the entire reason for the shape. The token is generated by MiseryRuntime at init and handed to the host bootstrap **in-process, by the runtime, at the moment the runtime loads it**. There is no discovery path and no way for a mod to obtain it from disk or environment.

2. **One handle.** `MbHandle` is `uint64` laid out `kind:8 | slot:24 | tag:32`, `0` always invalid. The tag is CSPRNG-drawn and **never reused for a slot**; a slot whose tag space is exhausted is permanently retired, so there is no ABA. **Mod slots are never recycled at all** — a mod id, once loaded, owns its slot for the process lifetime. That single rule kills mod-handle ABA, makes identity stable for diagnostics, and makes off-thread logging safe against a concurrent teardown (see THREADING).

3. **One ownership ledger.** Every resource a mod acquires pushes one `FOwned{kind, release_fn, subsystem, payload}` node onto its slot's intrusive LIFO chain. Unload walks that chain once, in reverse-insertion order. Adding a subsystem in 2031 means pushing a thunk, not editing the unload path.

4. **One callback shape, cookie-only.** `MbTrampolineFn(op, cookie, call_handle, MbErr*)`. `MB_Callback` **does not carry a function pointer** — this is the single most important graft from Handle Wall. Subscriptions store only a `uint64 cookie`. The one and only native-held managed address is installed by `misery.host`'s `set_trampoline`, once, from the never-collectible host ALC. A mod P/Invoking the table *cannot express* "native holds an address in my assembly," because the parameter does not exist.

5. **One payload — the bag.** A generational `MbHandle` of kind `Bag` plus two tagged accessors. Events, console invocations, service arguments and results, item definitions, settings-changed notifications: all bags. No struct crosses, no array crosses, no raw `const void*` payload pointer is ever handed to mod code, and adding a field is not an ABI change. This deletes Lattice's `where T : unmanaged` constraint (which did not compile against its own framework events) and its no-strings-in-events limitation in one move.

6. **One capability mechanism.** Named, independently versioned function tables — `misery.core`, `misery.events`, `misery.input`, `misery.settings`, `misery.services`, `misery.items`, `misery.console`, `misery.diagnostics`, `misery.host`. `misery.items` can reach v3 while `misery.core` sits at v1 for a decade. Optional subsystems reach C# **only** through `ctx.TryGet<T>(out T)` — there is no `Require<T>()` and no property to null-deref, so using an ungranted capability is a compile-time impossibility rather than a runtime exception.

THE FIVE STRUCTURAL RULES THAT MAKE IT UNBREAKABLE:
- **Owner first, always.** Every function in every table — including reads — takes `MbHandle owner` as its first parameter. `MB_E_NOT_OWNER` is reachable everywhere. This is the axis Handle Wall could not check at all and Lattice checked only on writes.
- **No aggregate by value, anywhere, including the frozen root.** Strings are `(const char* ptr, int32_t len)` pairs. `MbErr` crosses by pointer. This deletes the whole calling-convention question and the `sizeof(MB_Field) == 32` class of error, and makes the C# binding trivially blittable `delegate* unmanaged[Cdecl]<...>`.
- **No arrays cross.** Anything list-shaped is `*_count` + `*_at`, or a bag. Capability requirements are declared one call at a time (`mod_require_capability`), which is exactly this rule paying for itself.
- **No allocator crosses.** In-pointers borrowed for the call; out-buffers caller-allocated with a `*out_len = required` / `MB_E_BUFFER_TOO_SMALL` probe. There is no `mb_free` in the header because nothing is handed over.
- **Errors never unwind.** Every native entry is `noexcept` with a catch-all → `MB_E_MANAGED_FAULT`/internal; the managed trampoline body is entirely inside one `try/catch(Exception)`.

WHAT WAS DELETED OUTRIGHT, and why each deletion closes a named fatal flaw:
- `mod_open(mod_id)` from the mod-reachable table (Leased Context's identity-forgery primitive) → `mod_begin` lives in `misery.host`, which `acquire_capability` refuses to any owner that is not the host handle.
- The per-callback function pointer (Lattice's contradiction of its own REJECTED #3).
- The raw `const void* payload` handed to callbacks (Lattice) → bag handle.

/* ===========================================================================
 * mbpl_abi.h -- the ENTIRE native surface of the MBPL bridge. C99, no C++.
 *
 * ONE EXPORT. ONE ROOT (32 bytes, FROZEN FOREVER). ALL SCALARS. ALL HANDLES.
 *
 * THE FIVE RULES, none of which has an exception anywhere in this file:
 *   R1 NO AGGREGATE IS PASSED OR RETURNED BY VALUE. Strings are
 *      (const char* ptr, int32_t len) pairs. Structs cross by pointer only.
 *   R2 NO ARRAY CROSSES. Lists are *_count + *_at, or a bag handle.
 *   R3 NO ALLOCATOR CROSSES. `const char*` in is BORROWED for the duration of
 *      the call; `char*` out is CALLER-ALLOCATED and always receives the
 *      REQUIRED length in *out_len (too small => MB_E_BUFFER_TOO_SMALL, nothing
 *      written). There is no mb_free, because nothing is handed over.
 *   R4 EVERY CALL TAKES `MbHandle owner` FIRST -- reads included. "This handle
 *      is not yours" is therefore expressible and enforced everywhere.
 *   R5 NOTHING BUT MbStatus IS RETURNED. Data leaves through out-params. Only
 *      MbAcquireRoot returns a pointer, to a process-lifetime-immutable static.
 *
 * WITHIN A CAPABILITY MAJOR: functions are APPEND-ONLY. Never reordered, never
 * removed, never retyped. A breaking change is a NEW table served alongside the
 * old one until sunset. Enforced by a golden-file offset/signature test in CI.
 * =========================================================================== */
#ifndef MISERY_MBPL_ABI_H
#define MISERY_MBPL_ABI_H
#include <stdint.h>

#define MB_ABI_VERSION 1u

#if defined(_WIN32)
#  define MB_CALL   __cdecl
#  define MB_EXPORT __declspec(dllexport)
#else
#  define MB_CALL
#  define MB_EXPORT __attribute__((visibility("default")))
#endif

/* ---------------------------------------------------------------- status -- */
typedef int32_t MbStatus;                       /* 0 == OK, < 0 == failure */
#define MB_OK 0
#define MB_ERR(sub, code) \
    ((MbStatus)(int32_t)(0x80000000u | ((uint32_t)(sub) << 16) | (uint16_t)(code)))
#define MB_FAILED(s) ((s) < 0)
#define MB_SUB(s)    ((uint16_t)((((uint32_t)(s)) >> 16) & 0x7FFFu))
#define MB_CODE(s)   ((uint16_t)(((uint32_t)(s)) & 0xFFFFu))

enum MbSubsystem {
  MB_SUB_CORE = 1, MB_SUB_LOG = 2, MB_SUB_GT = 3, MB_SUB_EVENTS = 4,
  MB_SUB_INPUT = 5, MB_SUB_SETTINGS = 6, MB_SUB_SERVICES = 7, MB_SUB_ITEMS = 8,
  MB_SUB_CONSOLE = 9, MB_SUB_DIAG = 10, MB_SUB_HOST = 11, MB_SUB_MANAGED = 12
};

#define MB_E_INVALID_ARG      MB_ERR(MB_SUB_CORE,  1)
#define MB_E_STALE_HANDLE     MB_ERR(MB_SUB_CORE,  2)  /* tag/slot mismatch */
#define MB_E_HANDLE_KIND      MB_ERR(MB_SUB_CORE,  3)
#define MB_E_NOT_OWNER        MB_ERR(MB_SUB_CORE,  4)  /* R4 -- reachable everywhere */
#define MB_E_WRONG_THREAD     MB_ERR(MB_SUB_CORE,  5)
#define MB_E_QUIESCING        MB_ERR(MB_SUB_CORE,  6)
#define MB_E_BUFFER_TOO_SMALL MB_ERR(MB_SUB_CORE,  7)
#define MB_E_NAMESPACE        MB_ERR(MB_SUB_CORE,  8)
#define MB_E_ALREADY          MB_ERR(MB_SUB_CORE,  9)
#define MB_E_NOT_FOUND        MB_ERR(MB_SUB_CORE, 10)
#define MB_E_TYPE             MB_ERR(MB_SUB_CORE, 11)
#define MB_E_LIMIT            MB_ERR(MB_SUB_CORE, 12)
#define MB_E_REENTRANCY       MB_ERR(MB_SUB_CORE, 13)  /* nested dispatch depth > 8 */
#define MB_E_SEALED           MB_ERR(MB_SUB_CORE, 14)
#define MB_E_UNDECLARED       MB_ERR(MB_SUB_CORE, 15)  /* key/method not in the schema */
#define MB_E_CAP_UNKNOWN      MB_ERR(MB_SUB_CORE, 16)
#define MB_E_CAP_MAJOR        MB_ERR(MB_SUB_CORE, 17)
#define MB_E_CAP_MINOR        MB_ERR(MB_SUB_CORE, 18)
#define MB_E_CAP_NOT_GRANTED  MB_ERR(MB_SUB_CORE, 19)  /* not declared in mod.json */
#define MB_E_CAP_SUNSET       MB_ERR(MB_SUB_CORE, 20)
#define MB_E_ABI_UNSUPPORTED  MB_ERR(MB_SUB_CORE, 21)
#define MB_E_DENIED           MB_ERR(MB_SUB_CORE, 22)  /* host-only surface */

/* kind:8 | slot:24 | tag:32.  0 is ALWAYS invalid, for every kind.

 * exhausted is retired permanently. There is therefore no ABA, and blind
 * handle-guessing is a 2^32 search PER SLOT rather than a small-integer probe.
 * The OWNER is not in the handle: the slot record carries owner_slot + epoch,
 * so revoking a mod's entire handle set is one epoch increment.
 * A MOD SLOT IS NEVER RECYCLED -- a mod_id owns its slot for process lifetime.
 */
typedef uint64_t MbHandle;
#define MB_H_KIND(h) ((uint8_t)(((h) >> 56) & 0xFFu))
enum MbKind {
  MB_KIND_NONE = 0, MB_KIND_MOD = 1, MB_KIND_BAG = 2, MB_KIND_SUB = 3,
  MB_KIND_CHANNEL = 4, MB_KIND_ACTION = 5, MB_KIND_SETTING = 6,
  MB_KIND_SERVICE = 7, MB_KIND_SERVICE_USE = 8, MB_KIND_ITEM = 9,
  MB_KIND_COMMAND = 10, MB_KIND_LOGCH = 11
};

enum MbModState { MB_MOD_LOADING = 0, MB_MOD_LIVE = 1, MB_MOD_QUIESCING = 2,
